title: The Monks Who Kept the Books
standfirst: How a few quiet scriptoria carried ancient learning through the early Middle Ages.
body: When the western Roman Empire fell apart in the fifth century, much of its learning was at risk. Libraries were scattered, schools closed and books, which were expensive and fragile, were lost. That anything survived owes a great deal to monks working in cold rooms with quill and ink.

A book had to be copied by hand, letter by letter, onto prepared animal skin. A single large volume could take a scribe many months. Mistakes crept in, and later scribes sometimes copied the mistakes along with the text. Yet without this slow labour, many ancient works would not exist at all.

Some of the most important centres were in the British Isles. Monasteries in Ireland and Northumbria became famous for their scholars and their beautifully decorated books. Bede, writing at Jarrow in the early eighth century, produced history, science and commentary that were read across Europe.
These communities did not only preserve. They taught, corrected and argued. Learning moved between monasteries along with the monks themselves.

Viking raids from the late eighth century fell hard on rich, undefended monasteries, and many books were lost. The survival of what remains is often a matter of luck: a manuscript carried to safety, or a library that happened to be spared.
The next time someone calls the period the Dark Ages, it is worth remembering the people who spent their lives making sure the light did not go out.
